extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, classics, and writers studying or composing Socratic-style dialogues
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or analysing a Socratic philosophical dialogue that explores ethical concepts by staged argument, interlocutor challenge, and thought-experiment illustration. Emphasises methods for probing definitions, isolating cases, and moving from collective (State) to individual analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socratic question-and-answer (elenchus) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use persistent questioning and cross-examination to expose assumptions and force interlocutors to clarify their positions (e.g., Socrates asking whether he wishes 'really to persuade us' and pressing definitions and consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dialogue advances by pointed questions that require interlocutors to refine claims, admit premises, or face contradictions. Use short, focused questions to reveal gaps and then follow up on consequences; allow respondents space to propose revisions or new defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed from the greater to the lesser (state-to-individual analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze a moral quality first at the larger, more visible level (the State), then at the individual level: 'since a State is larger than an individual... proceeding from the greater to the lesser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an aggregated or institutional model to make features of the virtue/vice easier to see, then map those structures back onto the individual's soul or character. This scaffold helps render abstract traits concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify goods as conceptual framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the inquiry by sorting goods into three classes: (1) desired for themselves only, (2) desired both for themselves and results, (3) desired only for results — then ask which class the virtue belongs to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by explicitly distinguishing types of value (intrinsic, mixed, instrumental) to clarify interlocutors' assumptions about why one should pursue a thing. Use this taxonomy to test whether the target virtue is intrinsically valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thought-experiments and myths (Gyges' ring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce vivid hypothetical or mythical cases (e.g., the ring of Gyges that makes its wearer invisible) to test what people would do if constraints were removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy a concrete, memorable scenario to force readers/interlocutors to imagine extreme freedom and reveal presumed motivations. Ensure the experiment isolates the variable you want to test (e.g., absence of detection/punishment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate idealized extremes for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare perfectly just and perfectly unjust lives by imagining 'the unjust man be entirely unjust, and the just man entirely just' with no mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create extreme, cleaned-up cases (no mixed motives, full capacities) so the moral comparison isn't muddied by contingencies. State the assumptions clearly (e.g., reputation, power, skill) so the thought-experiment is fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require distinction between being just and seeming just
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly separate internal virtue from external reputation: 'there must be no seeming... let him be clothed in justice only, and have no other covering.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing moral claims, control for reputational incentives. Make characters who appear one way but are the opposite (or vice versa) to assess the intrinsic value of the virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role-play multiple perspectives and devil's-advocate moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Have interlocutors adopt opposing stances (e.g., Glaucon praising injustice, Adeimantus adding cultural/poetic arguments) to bring out objections and cultural assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cast characters to voice common objections, cultural testimonies, and rhetorical pressures. Let them present the strongest form of the counterargument to sharpen the dialectic and compel deeper analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude extrinsic rewards when testing intrinsic worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask interlocutors to 'setting aside their rewards and results' evaluate what justice and injustice are 'in themselves' — focus on intrinsic effects on the possessor's soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly bracket off consequences like honour, wealth, and afterlife rewards to test whether the target quality is good independent of instrumental benefits. State this constraint early to avoid equivocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogies and illustrative comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ analogies (e.g., short-sighted reader reading larger letters first) to explain methodological moves or to make abstract steps intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose simple, concrete analogies that map closely to the argumentative structure you want to justify. Make the mapping explicit so readers follow why the analogy supports the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a model society (thought experiment of city) from basic needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an imagined city arising 'out of the needs of mankind' — specify roles, division of labour, markets, and institutions — to make justice visible as social structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground the ethical inquiry in vivid social/world-building: enumerate necessary occupations, institutions (marketplace, money), and interdependencies. Use the city's structure to reveal where just relations must reside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalate from simple necessities to complex institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with elementary human needs (food, shelter, clothing) and progressively add specialized occupations, merchants, sailors, markets, and money to show how complexity produces sites for justice/injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the narrative unfold stepwise so each institutional addition introduces new moral questions. This progressive elaboration clarifies how ethical concepts scale with social complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use poetic and cultural authorities as rhetorical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite poets and traditions (Hesiod, Homer, Musaeus, Orpheus) to present prevailing cultural testimonies about virtue and its rewards or punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring in authoritative voices to represent societal beliefs you intend to investigate or refute; recount their images and promises to show the contrast between popular opinion and philosophical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage narrative detail and sensory description to humanize abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include concrete sensory and domestic details (diet, garlands, cakes, market-places) to make the imagined city and its citizens palpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, everyday detail to anchor abstract ethical debate in lived experience; this helps readers empathize and see how ethical claims affect real lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and answer skeptical rejoinders
rubrics_metrics.description: Preface the inquiry by acknowledging strong counterarguments (e.g., 'the many think justice is troublesome...') and invite their fullest expression before rebutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage interlocutors to voice the hardest objections (including culturally persuasive ones) and treat them seriously; this strengthens any subsequent defense and demonstrates fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use internal methodological signposting
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly tell readers the plan and stages of inquiry ('First... Secondly... And thirdly...') so the argument's architecture is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a roadmap for complex investigations: enumerate steps, state aims (nature of justice; whether men practice it willingly; comparative value of lives), and return to the plan as you progress.
